questions.stem: What forms when an aqueous carboxylic acid reacts with a reactive metal?

options.explanation: Metals displace hydrogen from the acid, leaving the metal salt behind.
Carbon dioxide belongs to the carbonate pattern, not to metals.
Water pairs with carbonates; the metal route releases hydrogen instead.
Ester-making needs an alcohol, which plays no part here.

questions.stem: Which set of products comes from a carboxylic acid plus a metal carbonate?

options.text: A salt, water and carbon dioxide
options.explanation: The carbonate supplies the carbon that leaves as the gas, and water forms alongside.
That pair is the metal pattern; carbonates never release hydrogen.
No oxygen gas is released in either pattern.
Ester-making needs an acid catalyst and an alcohol, not a carbonate.

questions.stem: How do the names of salts from carboxylic acids always end?

options.explanation: The oic acid ending converts to anoate when the acid becomes a salt.
The ide ending belongs to simple salts such as sodium chloride.
The oic acid ending marks the unreacted acid, not its salts.
The yl ending belongs to the alcohol part of ester names.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid reacts with magnesium. Which salt forms?

options.explanation: The metal name fronts the anoate ending taken from ethanoic acid.
The ide ending is never used for these salts.
Methanoate salts trace back to methanoic acid, a one-carbon member.
The acid group survives inside the salt; only its hydrogen is replaced.

questions.stem: Butanoic acid reacts with potassium carbonate. What is the salt called?

options.explanation: The metal supplies the first word and the four-carbon acid supplies the anoate ending.
The anoate ending is the fixed rule for this family.
Ethanoate traces back to the two-carbon acid, not the four-carbon one.
That is the reactant; the reaction consumes it and builds a new salt.

questions.stem: In the equation 2CH3COOH + Mg gives (CH3COO)2Mg + H2, why are two acid molecules needed?

options.text: The magnesium ion needs two ethanoate groups to balance its charge
options.explanation: Magnesium carries a 2+ charge, so two singly-charged ethanoate ions partner it.

options.text: One acid molecule is too heavy to react alone
options.explanation: Mass has nothing to do with it; charge balance drives the ratio.

options.text: Hydrogen only forms when acid is in excess
options.explanation: Hydrogen forms whatever the amount; the ratio is set by charges.

options.text: The second molecule acts as a catalyst
options.explanation: Neither acid molecule is recovered unchanged, so neither is a catalyst.

questions.stem: Which observation confirms the carbonate reaction of a carboxylic acid?

options.text: Fizzing as carbon dioxide is released
options.explanation: The carbonate pattern always releases the gas, which shows as effervescence.

options.text: A colour change from orange to green
options.explanation: That observation belongs to dichromate oxidations, not carbonates.

options.text: A smarting smell of the ester forming
options.explanation: No ester forms when a carbonate meets the acid.

options.text: A blue flame appearing above the mixture
options.explanation: Nothing burns in an acid-carbonate mixture.

questions.stem: Which formula is magnesium ethanoate written correctly?

options.explanation: The bracket doubles the ethanoate group onto the single magnesium ion.
Without the bracket the charges do not balance.
The methyl part of the group has been lost entirely.
The subscript sits on the wrong side; two groups partner one metal.

questions.stem: What does the gas tested in the carbonate reaction turn limewater into?

options.text: It turns limewater milky, proving carbon dioxide
options.explanation: The cloudy limewater test is the standard proof for carbon dioxide.

options.text: It burns with a squeaky pop, proving hydrogen
options.explanation: The pop test identifies hydrogen, which carbonates do not release here.

options.text: It relights a glowing splint, proving oxygen
options.explanation: Oxygen is not among the products of an acid-carbonate reaction.

options.text: It bleaches damp litmus, proving chlorine
options.explanation: Chlorine plays no part in this reaction.

questions.stem: In the butanoic acid equation, what does COOK at the end of CH3CH2CH2COOK represent?

options.text: The potassium ion taking the place of the acidic hydrogen
options.explanation: Metals replace the acid hydrogen to build the salt, so K closes the chain.

options.text: A cooking abbreviation left in the formula
options.explanation: The letters are element symbols: carbon, oxygen, potassium.
The salt is a solid dissolved in water, not a gas.

options.text: An unreacted piece of the carbonate
options.explanation: The carbonate has been broken apart; potassium now sits in the salt.
